variants.name: async/await returning Task<T> (Task-based Asynchronous Pattern)
variants.implementation_notes: C# makes the pattern syntax: an async method returning Task<T> is the promise-future pair, the compiler-generated state machine is the write end and the returned Task is the read end, while await is how a consumer collects the value and the synchronization context or task scheduler decides where the continuation runs. The Task can also be stored, passed and combined by hand (Task.WhenAll/WhenAny), which is the result-as-a-value form; TAP is Microsoft's prescribed shape for new code and supersedes the Begin/End (APM) and event-based (EAP) patterns.
pitfalls: async void is for event handlers only: its failures cannot be awaited or caught by the caller, which is why TAP prescribes returning Task even when there is no value.

Blocking on a context-bound task (.Result, .Wait(), GetAwaiter().GetResult()) can deadlock when the continuation needs the thread that is blocked - use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code and keep blocking at the very top of the call stack.

variants.name: TaskCompletionSource bridge around a callback API (manual promise)
variants.idiom_name: TaskCompletionSource<T> completed from a callback (or TaskFactory.FromAsync)
variants.implementation_notes: When an API does not return a Task - an APM Begin/End pair, an event, a raw callback - the promise is written by hand: create a TaskCompletionSource<T>, hand out its Task, and resolve it from the callback with TrySetResult, TrySetException or TrySetCanceled, exactly as the documented TaskFactory.FromAsync wrapper does for Begin/End pairs. The TCS is the single-assignment container, the Task is the read end, and the compiler is not involved; choose this for interop rather than as the default shape of new asynchronous APIs.
pitfalls: Resolve through TrySet* when the callback can fire more than once (an event raised repeatedly, a timeout racing completion): the Set* methods throw once the source is completed.
RunContinuationsAsynchronously matters: without it the completing callback's thread runs every continuation inline, so a slow awaiter blocks the producer.
